requirements.requirement: Deliver a copy of traffic node1 exchanges with node2 to node3, so a capture on node3 shows those packets even though addressed elsewhere
requirements.summary: Baseline capture on node3 showed 0 packets for node1<->node2 traffic (cmd-eadb297baa0445b2). After installing nftables `ip mirror` table with dup rules on node1 covering both directions (node1->node2 via output hook, node2->node1 via prerouting hook) (cmd-c5611b0faf49439e), a fresh capture on node3 showed both ICMP echo request and reply between 10.100.189.10 and 10.100.189.11, still addressed to each other, arriving on node3's interface (cmd-f9ff2d475f8d40f3). The rules match generic IP addresses (not protocol-restricted), so they cover node1<->node2 traffic broadly, verified here with ICMP as a representative protocol.

requirements.requirement: node1<->node2 traffic keeps flowing as it did before, unaffected by the mirroring
requirements.summary: Ping from node1 to node2 shows 0% packet loss and consistent RTT both immediately after enabling the mirror rules (cmd-4f4279ef88f44eba) and repeatedly after each of the three subsequent node restarts (cmd-8739da5889ae4683, cmd-ed251865267f4a8a, cmd-4ba5d21acef74194), confirming the real traffic path is undisturbed by duplication.

requirements.requirement: Mirroring configuration persists (survives reboot) so the solution is durable, not just a live-session hack
requirements.summary: The mirror table was appended to /etc/nftables.conf and nftables.service enabled with syntax validated (cmd-90913c6633f442ab). After node1's actual restart, `nft list table ip mirror` shows the identical rules still active with nftables.service reported active (cmd-57dc93e545f242d2), and a fresh node3 capture after the restart again shows mirrored ICMP traffic (cmd-f7a0e492709b43a2).

overall_summary: The executor delivered a working traffic-mirroring solution: nftables `dup` rules on node1 clone node1<->node2 IP traffic (both directions) to node3's address over eth0, directly confirmed by a before/after tcpdump comparison on node3 showing 0 packets at baseline and mirrored, originally-addressed ICMP traffic afterward. Ping evidence confirms the original node1<->node2 path is unaffected, both immediately after configuration and after all three nodes were restarted. The configuration was persisted via /etc/nftables.conf and nftables.service, and its survival was directly demonstrated by a real node1 reboot with matching rule state afterward. The mandatory provider-wide restart protocol was executed thoroughly for all three nodes with pre-restart baselines, reboot acknowledgements, changed boot IDs, and recovered connectivity/mirroring state, consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshots. The main blemish is a newly-failed SONiC system-health.service on node1 after its restart that was not investigated, plus a few small low-risk leftover evidence files (pcap/pid) on node3.
limitations: Mirroring was verified using ICMP traffic only; no test with TCP/UDP or non-IP traffic was captured to confirm broader protocol coverage, though the nftables rules are not protocol-restricted.

A new failed systemd unit (system-health.service) appeared on node1 after its restart and was not investigated by the executor; the root cause (mirroring config vs. unrelated SONiC platform behavior) is not established from the evidence.
Small residual evidence files (/tmp/mirror4.pcap, /tmp/td4.pid) remain on node3 after the run; low risk but not cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing actions were purposeful: initial iptables TEE attempt (cmd-4c80b69fba6047b8, cmd-d69a455ad50b4fdf) failed to move packets onto the wire and was cleanly flushed (cmd-dabf7dc641f4417f) before switching to the working nftables approach; a first `nft add table inet mirror` attempt failed with 'unsupported family' and was deleted in the very next command before the successful `ip mirror` table was created (cmd-c5611b0faf49439e). Several exploratory tcpdump captures directly on node1 (cmd-c8fd52c167b74e9c, cmd-9f28c4041abb4c02, cmd-16b0982362c44e24, cmd-9456dab3f51e4bfd, cmd-36ac119612fd4a2c, cmd-f5dbe3f6fab247b0) were diagnostic attempts to validate capture tooling, producing temp log/pcap files that do not appear in the after-executor node1 temp-file listing (likely cleared by the node1 reboot, since /tmp is typically volatile) — no lasting residue. On node3, sequential mirror*.pcap and td*.pid files were created for iterative evidence captures; only /tmp/mirror4.pcap and /tmp/td4.pid remain in the final snapshot — small, low-risk, non-sensitive leftover evidence files that were not cleaned up. Notably, after node1's restart a new failed unit appears that was not present in the before-prepare baseline: system-health.service (SONiC system health monitor) is now failed, which was not investigated or remediated by the executor and is an uncorrected regression coinciding with the mandated restart.
